alalal-e18128-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 7: whether the power of tyrants must be obeyed.

alalal-e18128-d1e113.summary: States the last question: whether tyrants, whom Boethius calls invaders with only usurped power, must be obeyed.

alalal-e18128-d1e126.summary: Argument for obedience: there is no power except from God, and whoever resists power resists God's ordinance.

alalal-e18128-d1e138.summary: Nebuchadnezzar had only usurped power over the Jews, yet Jeremiah urged obedience to him.

alalal-e18128-d1e156.summary: Pilate had only usurped power over the Lord, yet the Lord said it was given from above, and obeyed by not resisting.

alalal-e18128-d1e177.summary: Contrary: what is usurped is seized outside the order of law; we are not bound to obey it but rather to resist, lest the usurper lose his soul by seizing what is not his.

alalal-e18128-d1e190.summary: Likewise, the cross is preached against barbarians invading the Church's rights and peace, so such power must be resisted.

alalal-e18128-d1e199.summary: Solution: power is either ordained, according to the grades of ecclesiastical or civil law, and must not be resisted as to obedience; or usurped, the power of the Lord's scourge, which must not be resisted in the sense of refusing to bear it if God wills it, but may be resisted as to obedience when possible, since it is iniquitous and iniquity is always to be resisted. The first authorities concern bearing the scourge: God willed to scourge the Jews, as revealed to Jeremiah, and laid the chastisement of our peace on Christ, which is why Pilate's power was 'given from above', not because he ruled the Jews or Christ justly.
claims: Ordained power must be obeyed, but usurped tyrannical power may be resisted as to obedience.
God's permission of tyranny as a scourge must be borne patiently, without conferring legitimacy on the tyrant.

alalal-e18128.summary: Article 7, the last of Book II, asks whether tyrants with usurped power must be obeyed. Arguments for obedience cite Romans 13, Jeremiah's counsel to serve Nebuchadnezzar, and Christ's submission to Pilate. Arguments for resistance cite the illegitimacy of usurpation and crusades against invaders of the Church. Albert distinguishes power ordained by the grades of ecclesiastical or civil law, which must be obeyed, from usurped power, which is iniquitous and may be resisted as to obedience where possible. Insofar as God permits a tyrant as a scourge, the affliction must be borne patiently. This is the sense of the cases of Jeremiah and Pilate, whose power was 'from above' as a scourge, not as just rule.
claims: Legitimately ordained power must be obeyed, but usurped power may be resisted as to obedience.
A tyranny permitted by God as a scourge must be endured, which does not make the tyrant legitimate.
